summary: This document describes uniform patterns for building HTTP URLs to retrieve registration information from Regional Internet Registries and Domain Name Registries, using RESTful web access. These patterns define the query syntax of the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP). It obsoletes RFC 7482.

plainLanguage.summary: If you want to look up who registered a website, you need to know how to ask. This document says exactly how to write the web address for that question.

subtitle: The URL patterns clients use to look up who holds an IP network, AS number, domain, nameserver or contact.

tldr.problem: WHOIS has no standard command structure, no standard output or error format, no internationalization support and no support for user identification, authentication or access control.
tldr.mechanism: RDAP queries are plain HTTP GET or HEAD requests. A base URL from the IANA bootstrap registry is combined with a path segment such as ip, autnum, domain, nameserver, entity or help, or with a search form such as domains?name=example*.com.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9082 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 7482. It defines only the query side; the JSON answers are defined in RFC 9083.

sections.title: Why RDAP Queries Exist
sections.content:
This document specifies a way to query registration data using a RESTful web service and uniform query patterns. The service runs over HTTP, and these patterns define the query syntax of the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP). It addresses shortcomings of WHOIS, namely the lack of standardized command structures, standardized output and error structures, support for internationalization and localization, and support for user identification, authentication and access control.

The patterns purposefully do not cover every method used by Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) and Domain Name Registries (DNRs). They enable queries for networks by IP address, Autonomous System numbers by number, reverse DNS metadata by domain, nameservers by name, and entities (such as registrars and contacts) by identifier.

Servers may support only a subset. A server MUST return HTTP 501 (Not Implemented) for an unsupported query type. The patterns apply only to the HTTP GET and HEAD methods, since WHOIS-style services are read-only. The format of the results is left to RFC 9083, and provisioning and update functions are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: RDAP is a polite way to ask a public phone book who owns an internet address or name. This document only explains how to ask the question, not what the answer looks like.

sections.title: Exact-Match Lookups
sections.content:
Queries are built by taking a base URL from the IANA bootstrap registry (described in RFC 7484) and appending a path segment. If the base URL is https://example.com/rdap/, every query URL begins with it. The bootstrap registry has no information for objects outside a global namespace, such as entities and help, so a base URL must be known for those; RFC 8521 describes a practice for entities.

The lookup path segments are:

  • ip/<address> or ip/<prefix>/<length>: the most specific (smallest) network that completely encompasses the address or block. IPv6 text forms are accepted, and the zone identifier syntax of RFC 6874 MUST NOT be used.
  • autnum/<number>: an asplain Autonomous System number. If the number falls in a registered block, the block is the target; a single registration counts as a block of size 1.
  • domain/<name>: a fully qualified domain name, or a name in the in-addr.arpa or ip6.arpa zones for RIRs.
  • nameserver/<name>: a fully qualified host name.
  • entity/<handle>: an identifier whose syntax is specific to the registration provider.
  • help: usage information such as terms of service, privacy policy, rate-limiting policy and supported authentication methods.

For example, https://example.com/rdap/ip/192.0.2.0/24 finds the most specific network containing 192.0.2.0/24. A plain HEAD request can check whether an object exists without returning RDAP-encoded results.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of question has its own door: one for networks, one for numbers, one for website names. You walk through the right door and say the name you are curious about.

sections.title: Searches and Partial Matching
sections.content:
Search path segments use the plural form of the object (domains, nameservers, entities) followed by a question mark, a property name, an equals sign and a pattern. Unlike generic HTTP query strings, only one parameter is used at a time. Searches use GET.

  • Domains: domains?name=, domains?nsLdhName= and domains?nsIp=.
  • Nameservers: nameservers?name= and nameservers?ip=.
  • Entities: entities?fn= and entities?handle=.

Partial matching uses the asterisk. A pattern such as exam* matches example.com and example.net, while exam*.com matches example.com. A search string MUST NOT contain more than one asterisk. If a server does not support a particular style of partial match, it SHOULD return HTTP 422 (Unprocessable Entity). URLs must be properly encoded, so Bobby Joe* becomes Bobby%20Joe*.

Servers SHOULD NOT partially match combinations of Unicode characters where a legal combination is possible, and clients SHOULD NOT submit such partial searches.
sections.plainLanguage: A search is like asking the librarian for every book that starts with a few letters. The star means any ending is fine, but you can only use one star.

sections.title: Extending the Patterns
sections.content:
The document covers only a limited set of objects common to RIRs and DNRs. Custom path segments can be created by prefixing a segment with a unique identifier followed by an underscore. For example, a custom entity segment could be custom_entity. The process is described in RFC 7480.

A server MUST return an appropriate failure status code for a request with an unrecognized path segment. Future IETF documents may also add new query types.
sections.plainLanguage: If you invent your own kind of question, you put your own label in front of it. That way it never gets mixed up with the official ones.

sections.title: Internationalized Names and Encoding
sections.content:
Clients can submit an Internationalized Domain Name label either as a U-label (the Unicode form) or an A-label (the US-ASCII form); both are acceptable. Labels in one IDN SHOULD be all A-labels or all U-labels. A server that receives a mixture MAY convert all U-labels to A-labels and proceed, or MAY refuse the query. A server may match using either form, but one consistent form is likely more reliable.

A client sending non-ASCII characters converts them to UTF-8, applies any local case mapping, normalizes with Normalization Form C (NFC), and then percent-encodes the result. A server that gets invalid UTF-8 can stop and return HTTP 400 (Bad Request).

For DNS names, matching goes one label at a time, since one name can mix U-labels and Non-Reserved LDH labels. For everything else, servers compare using Normalization Form KC (NFKC) with case folding, and storing strings as Unicode is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Names in different alphabets can be written with fancy letters or with plain keyboard letters. The system accepts both, as long as you do not mix them in a single name.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Security services for these operations are described in RFC 7481. Searches generally need more server resources than basic lookups, which raises the risk of resource exhaustion and denial of service. The RFC suggests restricting search to identified and authorized clients, suspending or revoking the privileges of clients that misbehave, using the rate limiting from RFC 7480, and limiting how much information a search returns.

Search also raises privacy risk by disclosing relationships that are not otherwise obvious. For example, a search that returns IDN variants that do not explicitly match the pattern can reveal registered domain names that would not otherwise be available. The RFC notes that there may be no single static information-return policy for all clients, since client identity and authorization can affect how broad a response is.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting anyone search everything can overload the librarian and can reveal private connections. So the library may limit who searches and how much it hands back.

items.label: IP network
items.desc: ip/ADDRESS or ip/PREFIX/LENGTH; finds the most specific enclosing network.

items.label: Autonomous System
items.desc: autnum/ASN; a number inside a registered block resolves to that block.

items.label: Domain
items.desc: domain/NAME, including in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa names for RIRs.

items.label: Entity
items.desc: entity/HANDLE; handle syntax is specific to the provider.

items.label: Help
items.desc: Terms of service, privacy policy, rate limits and supported authentication methods.
